intro: Our wet-lab work is organized into Platform and Function. The scaffold-group contribution to Platform covers the construction and production of protein scaffolds, hydrogel preparation and characterization, cellular evaluation, and the ligation system. Within each experiment, the corresponding results and supporting figures are presented alongside the experimental description. Function is organized into magnetically responsive anisotropy, GAG retention and delivery.
platformHtml:
1 Hydrogel scaffold​

To produce the finished hydrogel, to verify the photocrosslinking and other properties of the scaffold protein, and to clarify how the protein sequence determines hydrogel performance, we carried out the expression and purification

of the scaffold protein, the photocrosslinking reaction and the measurement of

its mechanical properties. In parallel, we constructed plasmids encoding SELPs with different repeat numbers, produced and purified the corresponding proteins and fabricated hydrogels from them, compared their mechanical properties with one another, and thereby determined the effect of repeat number on hydrogel

properties; this work was combined with our modeling to build a more accurate

and reliable prediction system. We also tested the cytocompatibility of the hydrogel material in order to assess its safety.​

1.1 Design of the scaffold plasmid​

Scaffold plasmid design

Experiment

This study used the silk–elastin-like protein (SELP) sequence 2KY as the base scaffold. The basic repeat unit of 2KY is 171 bp in length, encodes 57 amino acids, and has the following sequence composition:​

(GAGAGS)₂–GRGDS–GKGVP–(GVGVP)₃–GYGVP–(GVGVP)₃​

The sequence contains both silk-like GAGAGS modules and elastin-like GVGVP modules, and introduces tyrosine (Tyr, Y), lysine (Lys, K) and the cell-adhesion- related RGD motif into the repeat unit.​

Results

Specifically, a BseRI recognition site (GAGGAG) was embedded in the GGGGS linker

14 bp upstream of the repeat array, and an AcuI recognition site (CTTCAG on the coding strand) was embedded in the GGSGGSSGS trailer 17 bp downstream. Both are type IIS restriction enzymes that cleave outside their recognition sequences:

BseRI cuts 10/8 nt and AcuI 16/14 nt away from the recognition site, each leaving a

2-nt 3′ overhang. The phases of the two flanking linkers were designed such that both overhangs are GG, identical to the first two bases of the repeat array.​

Consequently, the plasmid is digested with AcuI + XbaI and with BseRI + XbaI in parallel, the gene-containing half of each digest is recovered, and the two pieces are ligated. In a single cycle, this doubles the repeat array and reconstitutes the

plasmid, with no extra bases remaining at the junction and the reading frame

unchanged. Both enzyme sites remain outside the doubled array, so the cycle

can be repeated indefinitely (Figure 1.1.1).​

A key feature of this design is that the enzyme recognition sites lie within the flanking linkers and never within the repeat sequence itself. The approach is therefore not constrained by the codon degeneracy of glycine/alanine-rich sequences such as 2KY, which is precisely the obstacle that classical RDL cannot

overcome for such sequences.​

In addition, we reserved three docking sites for SnoopTag2 on the plasmid.

Their positions relative to the two cut sites determine the fate of the tag during doubling (Table 1.1.1):​

Table 1.1.1. Positions of the three SnoopTag2 docking sites relative to the cut sites, their behavior during a doubling round, and the resulting constructs.​

Tag insertion sitePosition relative to cut siteBehavior during a doubling roundResulting construct
N-terminus (before NdeI)Upstream of the BseRI cut siteNot duplicated; remains a single copyTag–[2KY-5]n
End of the gene (before the trailer)Upstream of the AcuI cut siteDuplicated together with the repeat unit[2KY-5-Tag]n
C-terminus (before the stop codon)Downstream of the AcuI cut siteNot duplicated; remains a single copy[2KY-5]n–Tag

In this project, we adopted the second site, such that each 2KY-5 block is followed

by one SnoopTag2. Scaffold length and interface number thereby become a jointly programmable quantity, rather than two variables that must be constructed separately.​

Accordingly, we obtained a single parental plasmid, pET19b-2KY5-RDL (6636 bp;

Figure 1.1.2), by whole-gene synthesis; all three other constructs were derived from it experimentally.​

1.2 Scaffold protein 2KY-5​

1.2.1 Expression of the scaffold protein 2KY-5​
Transformation and sequence verification

Experiment

The constructed plasmid encoding the 2KY-5 protein was transformed into E. coli

BL21(DE3).

Plasmid identity was verified by colony PCR. We used the T7 promoter and T7 terminator primers, which anneal outside the insert, as the forward and reverse primers. This primer pair is common to all constructs in this series, and the product size varies with the repeat number, so that the copy number can be read directly from the band position. The cultures were then sent for sequencing to verify that the sequence was correct.​

The expression strain was then inoculated into LB medium containing Amp and cultured to mid-logarithmic phase, after which expression was induced with 1 mM

IPTG (final concentration) for approximately 6 h. Cells were harvested and lysed by sonication, and the supernatant was collected. Samples of the culture before and after induction, the lysate supernatant and the lysate pellet were analyzed by SDS-

Results

The synthesized pET19b-2KY5-RDL was successfully transformed into E. coli

BL21(DE3), and colonies were obtained (Figure 1.2.1.1). Agarose gel electrophoresis of the PCR products showed a band at 1152 bp, consistent with the theoretical

size of 2KY-5 (Figure 1.2.1.2), and sequencing of the insert confirmed that its

sequence was correct.​

No band was present at the expected molecular weight before induction, whereas a band appeared after induction, demonstrating successful IPTG induction

without leaky expression (Figure 1.2.1.3). In addition, the target band was present in the lysate supernatant but faint in the pellet, indicating that cell lysis is a feasible method for the initial recovery of 2KY-5.​

1.2.2 Purification of the scaffold protein 2KY-5​
Optimization of inverse transition cycling

Experiment

Elastin-like proteins undergo an inverse temperature transition, denaturing and

aggregating at elevated temperature and redissolving upon cooling. On the basis of this behaviour, we selected inverse transition cycling (ITC) for the purification of the scaffold protein.​

Briefly, the lysate of the harvested cells was subjected repeatedly to high-salt, high- temperature denaturation and aggregation, collection of the pellet, and low- temperature dissolution in ultrapure water followed by collection of the supernatant, which completed the extraction of the scaffold protein.​

We determined the optimal ITC parameters through a two-factor gradient screen of the transition temperature and the transition salinity, and the purification performance was monitored by SDS-PAGE. The solution obtained after ITC was further subjected to ultrafiltration, which served to purify, concentrate and exchange the buffer, yielding a scaffold protein solution whose final solvent was water; the protein was then lyophilized to a powder, the storage form used for the subsequent preparation of hydrogel solutions.​

The purified supernatant was concentrated using ultrafiltration tubes with a 10-kDa molecular weight cut-off (3,500 × g, 30 min), and the protein concentrations before and after concentration were determined by the BCA assay.([6])​

Results

We performed a gradient screen of two parameters, the NaCl concentration of the buffer and the heating temperature. The results showed that raising the temperature had little effect on the purification yield, whereas the NaCl

concentration of the buffer was the more influential factor, and that the buffer containing 2 M NaCl gave the highest yield (Figure 1.2.2.1 and Figure 1.2.2.2). This trend is consistent with the reported regulation of the phase-transition temperature of elastin-like polypeptides by salt ions.([5])​

Subsequent purifications were carried out under the optimal conditions

identified (heating to 65 °C; PBS containing 2 M NaCl). Samples of the lysate supernatant, the supernatant after the high-temperature phase transition, the pellet obtained after cooling-induced redissolution, and the supernatant after cooling were collected during ITC and analyzed by SDS-PAGE to confirm the purification effect. Compared with the initial lysate supernatant, the contaminating protein bands were absent from the cooled supernatant collected after ITC, and the band corresponding to 2KY-5 was present only in the final solution, with almost no loss during the process, indicating excellent purification (Figure 1.2.2.3).​

The purified 2KY-5 supernatant was concentrated with an ultrafiltration tube to give approximately 5 mL of solution. The concentration factor between the samples before and after concentration was approximately 3.5, with essentially no protein loss (Figure 1.2.2.4).​

The solution was then dialyzed to remove residual salt, and the dialyzed solution was stored at −80 °C and lyophilized to a powder for storage. Based on the calculated yield, approximately 500 mg of protein was obtained per liter of bacterial culture. This is a high yield under the routine protein-induction conditions currently used in our laboratory, making the process suitable for further optimization of the production conditions toward industrial-scale mass production, and giving it high commercial value. The detailed workflow and equipment in our laboratory are shown in Figure 1.2.2.5.​

1.2.3 Photocrosslinking of 2KY-5 and preparation of the hydrogel​
Blue-light photocrosslinking

Experiment

Using the lyophilized scaffold protein powder obtained above, together with the photocrosslinker (C₃₀H₂₄Cl₂N₆Ru · 6H₂O/Na₂S₂O₈), we prepared a 10% (w/v) hydrogel precursor solution in PBS containing 2 mM ruthenium (Ru) and 20 mM sodium persulfate (SPS).​

The system was then irradiated with 450-nm blue light to initiate crosslinking. After

Results

The non-irradiated system flowed to the bottom of the tube upon inversion, whereas the irradiated system remained in place, demonstrating that the system

was fully crosslinked after 2 s of blue-light irradiation (Figure 1.2.3.2;

Supplementary Movies S1 and S2).​

Under visible light, the Ru/SPS system catalyses the formation of covalent dityrosine crosslinks between adjacent tyrosine residues.​

Before photoexcitation: the Ru/SPS hydrogel precursor solution flows when inverted. (S1) Video awaiting platform review

After photoexcitation: no flow when inverted, indicating successful gelation via crosslinking at tyrosine residues. (S2) Video awaiting platform review

1.2.4 Characterization of the hydrogel​
Hydrogel morphology

Experiment

In our project, 2KY-5 and 2KY-10 proteins were independently produced and purified in our laboratory, while samples of 2Y-5 and 2KY-16 were provided by Professor Hongwei Ouyang and Professor Wenwen Huang at our collaborating laboratory. We subsequently performed standardized characterization of all four proteins. Therefore, the production of 2Y-5 and 2KY-16 is not described further in the following sections. Scanning electron

microscopy (SEM) was first used to observe the hydrogel structure and pore size.​

Samples taken before and after gelation were then examined by three-dimensional

excitation–emission matrix (EEM) fluorescence spectroscopy in order to confirm

tyrosine crosslinking.​

With respect to mechanical properties, we performed frequency-sweep rheology,

compression tests and shear adhesion tests, from which mechanical parameters

such as the Young’s modulus of the hydrogels were obtained.​

Results

The two videos below demonstrate the shape and excellent elasticity of our hydrogel, as well as its strong adhesive properties.

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) showed that the hydrogel has an

interconnected, three-dimensional porous network with pores of varying size

(Figure 1.2.4.1). Such porous architecture may facilitate the diffusion of

nutrients and metabolites.​

To verify the chemical nature of the crosslinking, three-dimensional excitation–

emission matrix (EEM) fluorescence spectra of the precursor solution and the resulting hydrogel were recorded (Figure 1.2.4.2). The precursor solution showed a fluorescence peak at an excitation wavelength of approximately 280 nm and an emission wavelength of approximately 300–310 nm, corresponding to the intrinsic fluorescence of tyrosine. After gelation, the main fluorescence peak shifted to an excitation wavelength of approximately 330 nm and an emission wavelength of approximately 400 nm, with markedly increased intensity. Emission near 400 nm is

characteristic of dityrosine [9] ,suggesting that dityrosine crosslinks formed

between tyrosine residues upon illumination.​

310 nm to approximately 330/400 nm upon gelation.​

Frequency-sweep rheology (Figure 1.2.4.3) showed that, over the entire range of

0.1–100 rad/s, the storage modulus (G′) of all three hydrogels (2Y-5, 2KY-5 and 2KY-

16) exceeded the loss modulus (G″) by at least approximately two orders of magnitude and was essentially independent of frequency, indicating that

photocrosslinking produced a stable, predominantly elastic, solid-like

network. The G′ values of 2Y-5 and 2KY-5 were similar (approximately 2–3 kPa), whereas that of 2KY-16 reached approximately 20 kPa, nearly one order of

magnitude higher. We speculate that this may be related to the larger number of crosslinking sites provided by the longer scaffold chains and the resulting reduction in dangling chain ends (a hypothesis that remains to be tested experimentally).​

(G′) and loss modulus (G″) as a function of angular frequency for 2Y-5, 2KY-5 and 2KY-16.​

The stress–strain curves (Figure 1.2.4.4A) showed that, within a strain range of 0–

0.3, the stress of all three hydrogels increased nonlinearly with strain; the stress of

2KY-16 (approximately 23 kPa at a strain of 0.3) was clearly higher than that of

2Y-5 and 2KY-5 (approximately 15 kPa), whose curves nearly overlapped. The

Young’s moduli calculated accordingly were approximately 29 kPa for 2Y-5, 30 kPa for 2KY-5 and 53 kPa for 2KY-16; there was no significant difference between 2Y-5 and 2KY-5 (ns), whereas 2KY-16 was significantly higher than both (p < 0.001) (Figure

1.2.4.4B). Thus, increasing the repeat number from 5 to 16 effectively enhanced

the mechanical strength of the hydrogel.​

Figure 1.2.4.4. Stress–strain curves and Young’s moduli of the hydrogels. (A)

Stress–strain curves over a strain range of 0–0.3. (B) Young’s moduli. ns, not significant; ***, p < 0.001.​

In the shear adhesion test (Figure 1.2.4.5A), the shear force of all three hydrogels rose with displacement to a peak and then declined, with peak forces of approximately 11 N (2Y-5), 17 N (2KY-5) and 27.5 N (2KY-16). The resulting shear strengths were approximately 32, 42 and 91 kPa, respectively (no significant difference between 2Y-5 and 2KY-5; 2KY-16 significantly higher than both, p <

0.001) (Figure 1.2.4.5B). In addition, probing the hydrogel with a pipette tip

(Supplementary Movie S3) and adhering it to the surface of a culture dish

(Supplementary Movie S4) both demonstrated that the hydrogel has good

elasticity and adhesiveness.​

Figure 1.2.4.5. Shear adhesion performance of the hydrogels. (A) Shear force– displacement curves. (B) Shear strength. ns, not significant; ***, p < 0.001.​

Fabricated hydrogel and demonstration of elasticity. (S3) Video awaiting platform review

Demonstration of the hydrogel’s adhesive properties. (S4) Video awaiting platform review

1.3 Construction and production of hydrogels with different repeat numbers​

1.3.1 Plasmid construction, expression and purification of the scaffold protein 2KY-10​
Recursive doubling of the scaffold

Experiment

Taking the previously constructed 2KY-5 plasmid as the starting material, we constructed the corresponding 2KY-10 plasmid, in which the repeat number is doubled. Because SELP coding sequences are highly repetitive, doubling the repeat number is difficult to achieve by conventional PCR or homologous recombination.

We therefore adopted the plasmid reconstruction recursive directional ligation

(PRe-RDL) method, which is better suited to this situation (see Section 1.1).​

2KY-10 was not chemically synthesized but was obtained directly from pET19b-

2KY5-RDL by one round of PRe-RDL. The plasmid was divided into two aliquots:

one was double-digested with AcuI + XbaI (digest A) and the other with BseRI + XbaI

(digest B). All three enzymes are active at 37 °C in rCutSmart buffer and can therefore be used directly in double digestions. The digestion time was kept within

2 h and the enzyme amount did not exceed 10 U/µg to avoid the star activity of

AcuI; AcuI reactions were supplemented with S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). Digest

A yielded four fragments, from which the 1008-bp target fragment containing the scaffold gene was taken (fragment F); digest B yielded two fragments, from which the 6483-bp large fragment was taken (fragment G) and the 153-bp small fragment was discarded. The two target fragments were gel-purified separately, mixed in equimolar amounts, ligated with T4 DNA ligase at 16 °C overnight, and transformed into DH5α.​

Plasmid construction was then verified by colony PCR and sequencing. The target colony was picked for plasmid amplification: because this is a low-copy plasmid, streptomycin was added when the culture reached an OD of approximately 0.6 to promote plasmid amplification; the plasmid was then extracted with a plasmid midi-prep kit, and the plasmid concentration and purity were measured by

NanoDrop, both reaching satisfactory levels.​

The expression and purification of 2KY-10 followed the conditions used for 2KY-5

Results

2KY-10 was obtained directly from pET19b-2KY5-RDL by one round of PRe-RDL following the method described in Section 1.1, and the plasmid was successfully transformed into DH5α and BL21 (Figure 1.3.1.2).​

Single colonies were picked for colony PCR, and the band shifted upward from 1152 bp for 2KY-5 to 2007 bp (Figure 1.3.1.3); the difference of 855 bp corresponds exactly to one 2KY-5 unit, demonstrating successful doubling. Sequencing confirmed

that the repeat region consisted of 10 complete monomers.​

The purification results are shown in Figure 1.3.1.4: the purification was effective, with a yield of approximately 480 mg per liter of bacterial culture, close to that of

2KY-5.​

1.3.2 Plasmid construction, expression and purification of the scaffold proteins 2KY-5-Tag and 2KY-10-Tag​
Insertion of SnoopTag2

Experiment

Using the corresponding 2KY-5 and 2KY-10 plasmids as the starting materials, we introduced SnoopTag2 (KLGYIEFYKVEK; coding sequence of 36 bp) into both by site- directed insertion.​

This step cannot be accomplished by conventional single-fragment whole-plasmid amplification: the insertion point lies immediately adjacent to the repeat region, so that however the reverse primer is designed, its 3′ end falls within the repeat sequence and initiates extension from all five repeats simultaneously, generating a ladder of products that differ by 171 bp. At the scale of the 6.6-kb whole plasmid, these products cannot be separated, and deletion mutants would inevitably be mixed in.​

We therefore adopted Method 2 of the Mut Express II kit (two-fragment

amplification) and joined the two fragments by homologous recombination: an additional anchor, B, which introduces no mutation, was placed in a unique region outside the insertion point (upstream of NdeI), splitting the plasmid into two fragments that were amplified separately.​

After DpnI digestion, the two fragments were recombined using Exnase II at 37 °C for 30 min according to the ratio recommended in the manual (0.03 pmol of the longer fragment and 0.06 pmol of the shorter fragment) and transformed into

DH5α. Colony PCR was then performed, and plasmids giving the correct band were sequenced; all sequencing results were correct. The correctly sequenced 2KY-5-Tag and 2KY-10-Tag plasmids were transformed into E. coli BL21.​

Results

Taking 2KY-5-Tag as an example (the procedure for 2KY-10-Tag is the same), the two fragments were amplified separately by the method described in the Experiment section and analyzed by agarose gel electrophoresis, which showed that the amplified bands were all of the expected size; the fragments were then gel-purified

(Figure 1.3.2.1):​

1. B→I fragment (Anchor-BF + Snp-IR): the correct product should be 956 bp.​

2. I→B fragment (Snp-IF + Anchor-BR): the correct product should be 5792 bp.​

After recombination of the two fragments with Exnase II, the products were successfully transformed into DH5α to give single colonies on the plates. Plasmids were extracted in the same way and subjected to colony PCR, and plasmids giving the correct band were sequenced; all sequencing results were correct.​

The correctly sequenced 2KY-5-Tag and 2KY-10-Tag plasmids were transformed into E. coli BL21, and single colonies were successfully obtained (Figure 1.3.2.2);

both plasmids were thus successfully constructed and transformed.​

Protein expression was subsequently induced and the proteins were purified. The purification results are shown in Figure 1.3.2.3: the purification was effective, with yields of approximately 520 mg and 490 mg per liter of bacterial culture for 2KY-5-

Tag and 2KY-10-Tag, respectively, close to that of 2KY-5.​

Hydrogel scaffold — module summary

The scaffold workflow links plasmid construction, protein production and hydrogel characterization. The parental 2KY-5 construct supports recursive extension and SnoopTag2 insertion, while the expression and purification workflow is applied across the resulting scaffold series. Photocrosslinking, structural characterization and mechanical testing establish the material properties described above.

2 Safety and functional evaluation of the hydrogel​

2.1 Cytotoxicity assessment​

Cytotoxicity assessment

Experiment

The relative viability of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) after co-culture with the

SELP protein was measured by the CCK-8 assay. A control group, a blank group and treatment groups (5 µM and 10 µM) were set up, and three time points (24, 48 and

96 h) were examined. The experimental groups comprised a dressing-solution group and low- and high-concentration G-S groups (G-S low, stock solution diluted

Results

The CCK-8 results were as follows. At 24 h, the cell viability of the dressing-solution,

G-S low and G-S high groups was 125.1 ± 36.3%, 110.2 ± 12.4% and 100.7 ±

12.7%, respectively; at 48 h, 134.7 ± 3.2%, 103.0 ± 4.4% and 102.7 ± 4.7%; and at

72 h, 119.0 ± 15.5%, 98.6 ± 27.6% and 88.2 ± 17.6% (percentages relative to the control group; mean ± SD, n = 3).​

The mean viability of every group at every time point was not lower than 88%, above the 70% threshold defined in ISO 10993-5 (a reduction of cell viability by more than 30% is considered a cytotoxic effect).[10]. Overall, these results

indicate that the material is not markedly cytotoxic (Figure 2.1.1).​

SELP protein, measured by the CCK-8 assay at 24, 48 and 72 h. Percentages are relative to the control group (mean ± SD, n = 3).​

2.2 Functional validation in chondrocytes​

Chondrocyte gene-expression analysis

Experiment

Special Note : Our collaborating team, led by Professors Hongwei Ouyang and

Wenwen Huang, has an established and well-developed cartilage cell culture

system. Therefore, their team conducted the cartilage cell culture and functional

validation of SELP. Our team did not directly perform any biosafety-relevant

experimental procedures in this part of the project.​

To further evaluate the effect of the hydrogels on the chondrocyte phenotype (the chondrocytes were not cultured or validated by our own team; the SELP hydrogel materials were sent to a third party for evaluation, so no biosafety issue is involved), chondrocytes were co-cultured with the hydrogels (2Y-5, 2KY-5 and 2KY-

16), and the expression of cartilage-related genes was measured by qPCR (Figure

Results

The qPCR results after co-culture of the hydrogels with chondrocytes were as follows:​

Using the 2Y-5 group (a scaffold protein without lysine sites, constructed in our laboratory and not shown here for reasons of space) as the reference (relative expression set to 1), the expression of aggrecan (ACAN) and type II collagen (COL2) was significantly upregulated in both the 2KY-5 and 2KY-16 groups; SOX9 expression was upregulated to approximately 3.2–3.3-fold (p < 0.05), with no significant difference between the two groups. At the same time, the expression of type I collagen (COL1) decreased to approximately 0.17-fold and 0.13-fold (p < 0.001), with no significant difference between the two groups. Type X collagen (COLX) was elevated to approximately 2.7-fold in the 2KY-5 group (p < 0.05 compared with both the 2Y-5 and 2KY-16 groups), whereas there was no significant difference between the 2KY-16 and 2Y-5 groups.​

These results indicate that the 2KY hydrogels promote the expression of

cartilage matrix-related genes (ACAN, COL2 and SOX9) in chondrocytes and

suppress COL1 expression. Increased COL1 expression is a hallmark of the loss

of the cartilage phenotype (dedifferentiation) of chondrocytes in culture,([11])

and SOX9 is a key transcriptional activator of COL2 expression;([12]) this

expression profile is therefore conducive to maintaining the chondrocyte

phenotype. Among the groups, 2KY-16 had the stronger promoting effect on

ACAN and COL2 expression, indicating that to a certain extent the effect is

better as the repeat number increases, which makes it more suitable for our

clinical choice.​

Hydrogel evaluation — module summary

The cell experiments evaluate the hydrogel-related samples through CCK-8 measurements and cartilage-related gene expression. Together, these assays connect the material characterization to the cellular responses reported for the tested conditions.

3 Ligation system​

To verify that our ligation system is feasible and efficient and does not impair the

hydrogel scaffold or the functional modules, we first fused SnoopTag2 and

DogTag to sfGFP and SUMO, respectively, and placed the two fusion proteins together with SnoopLigase2 in a single system for the ligation reaction, which provided an initial validation of the normal function and efficiency of the system.

We then ligated SnoopTag2 and DogTag to the scaffold protein and to the functional modules, respectively, in order to verify the performance of the ligation system under realistic conditions; the resulting products can in turn be used to examine the effect of incorporating functional modules into the hydrogel scaffold.​

3.1 Expression of the ligation-system proteins

Expression of the ligation-system components

Experiment

Plasmids encoding SnoopTag2-sfGFP, SUMO-DogTag and SnoopLigase2 were separately transformed into E. coli BL21(DE3) for protein expression. The expression strains were inoculated into LB liquid medium containing kanamycin

(Kan) and cultured to mid-logarithmic phase, after which expression was induced with IPTG at a gradient of 0.1/0.25/0.5/1.0 mM. After culture at 16 °C for 16 h, a small volume of culture was lysed by sonication and subjected to small-scale purification by nickel-affinity chromatography. The lysates and the purified eluates were analyzed by Western blot using an anti-His primary antibody.​

Results

The Western blot results confirmed that all three target proteins were successfully induced, and the optimal induction concentrations of SnoopTag2-sfGFP, SUMO-

DogTag and SnoopLigase2 were 0.1 mM, 0.1 mM and 1.0 mM, respectively (Figure

3.1.1). Large-scale production was subsequently carried out under the optimal

conditions determined, and expression was good for all three proteins (Figure

3.1.2).​

SnoopTag2-sfGFP, SUMO-DogTag and SnoopLigase2 were expressed under the optimized induction conditions.​

3.2 Purification and dialysis of the ligation-system proteins​

Purification and protein concentrations

Experiment

The proteins were purified by nickel-affinity chromatography. The purified solutions of the three proteins were dialyzed in dialysis bags with a 3.5-kDa molecular weight cut-off. The dialysis buffer was PBS for SnoopTag2-sfGFP and

Results

After purification by nickel-affinity chromatography and dialysis (Figure 3.2.1), the final concentrations of the three protein solutions were: ​

SnoopTag2-sfGFP (30 kDa)- 1.33 mg/mL; ​

SnoopLigase2 (12.9 kDa)-0.66 mg/mL; ​ and SUMO-DogTag (14.7 kDa)- 0.60 mg/mL.​

3.3 Ligation reaction​

Time-course analysis of ligation

Experiment

Based on the measured protein concentrations, the reaction system was prepared with all three components at a final concentration of 25 µM, and the ligation reaction was carried out at room temperature (approximately 24 °C). Samples were taken at 10, 30 and 60 min after setting up the reaction, and the reactions were terminated by boiling. The individual components and the samples from the different reaction times were analyzed by SDS-PAGE.​

Results

The results showed that ligation had occurred within 10 min (a distinct ligation- product band of approximately 45 kDa appeared, consistent with the sum of SUMO-

DogTag at 14.7 kDa and SnoopTag2-sfGFP at 30 kDa) and was complete within 1 h

(the band of SUMO-DogTag, which was present in lower amount, disappeared), demonstrating that the ligation reaction is very rapid and efficient (Figure 3.3.1).​

Ligation system — module summary

The ligation workflow covers production and purification of the three components, followed by a time-course assay of the reaction. The results connect preparation of the ligation-system proteins with the formation of the ligation product shown in the original gel.

Platform summary

The scaffold-group work brings together a programmable protein scaffold, a hydrogel preparation workflow, material and cellular characterization, and a peptide ligation system. These experimental stages provide the basis for assembling and evaluating the platform described in this section.
